sections.title: Recognizing the species
sections.text: Lycoperdon perlatum Pers. (common puffball) forms a whitish, inverted pear-shaped fruit body, usually only a few centimetres tall. Its surface is covered with firm conical spines mixed with smaller granules; when these fall away, they leave round scars, sometimes in a reticulate pattern. At maturity the outer peridium opens at the top through a pore, releasing spores as a powder.

sections.title: Section and maturation
sections.text: A longitudinal section shows a fertile gleba that is initially white, firm and homogeneous, then turns yellow and finally olive-brown and powdery as it matures. Beneath it, the sterile subgleba is pale, spongy and chambered; it extends into the narrowed base, which may attach to fine mycelial cords. A thin, smooth inner wall surrounds the gleba beneath the spiny outer peridium.

sections.title: Habitat
sections.text: This saprotrophic species grows alone, scattered or in groups on soil and leaf litter in broadleaf or conifer woods, as well as in parks and gardens. It fruits mainly from late spring through autumn, depending on region. It differs from Lycoperdon pyriforme, which is smoother and associated with wood, by its prominent spines and usually terrestrial growth.

sections.title: Edibility and caution
sections.text: The DGfM and VAPKO lists include it among edible species, but only while young and while the gleba remains white. Before identification, make a full-length cut and check that the interior is homogeneous, with no outline of a cap, gills or stem; those structures inside an ‘egg’ may indicate a young Amanita still wrapped in its veil, potentially deadly. A page or photograph is not enough to decide whether to eat a wild mushroom: ask an expert to confirm it. Also avoid inhaling spore clouds from mature puffballs; rare cases of lycoperdonosis have been reported after inhalation of large quantities of puffball spores.

traits: Whitish, inverted pear-shaped fruit body, usually a few centimetres tall, with a narrowed sterile base
Outer peridium covered in firm conical spines and smaller granules; fallen spines leave round scars
At maturity, an apical pore opens in the wall to release olive-brown spore powder
In section, fertile gleba white and homogeneous when young, then yellow and olive-brown and powdery; lower sterile subgleba pale and spongy
Saprotrophic on soil and leaf litter in broadleaf or conifer woods, parks and gardens; fruits from spring to autumn depending on region
safetyNote: Only young specimens with a white, homogeneous gleba are considered edible. Cut each specimen fully lengthwise: the outline of a cap or stem beneath a wrapper may indicate a young Amanita, potentially deadly. Never eat a mushroom based on this page or a photo; have its identity confirmed. Do not inhale spore clouds from mature puffballs: rare cases of lycoperdonosis are associated with inhaling large quantities.
